title: Week 11 · Lesson 33: Cardiovascular Pharmacology I — Antihypertensive Therapy, RAAS & Diuretics
html:
PHASE 2 · ADVANCED PHARMACOLOGY

Week 11 — Lesson 33: Cardiovascular Pharmacology I — Antihypertensive Therapy, RAAS & Diuretics

FNP-level goal: Choose and monitor antihypertensive therapy by connecting blood-pressure physiology, compelling indications, patient risk, laboratory trends, and safe follow-up.

Learning Objectives

  • Connect antihypertensive classes to cardiac output, systemic vascular resistance, and extracellular volume.
  • Compare RAAS-active drugs, calcium-channel blockers, diuretics, and beta blockers by clinical role and key safety considerations.
  • Recognize how kidney function, potassium, sodium, volume status, pregnancy potential, and comorbidities affect selection and monitoring.
  • Distinguish chronic hypertension management from hypertensive emergency assessment.
  • Build a patient-centered monitoring and counseling plan instead of treating a single office blood-pressure value.

Part 1 — Begin With the Physiology

Blood pressure is influenced by:

Mean arterial pressure ≈ cardiac output × systemic vascular resistance.

Antihypertensive medications work by changing one or more of these variables:

  • Reducing vascular tone and systemic vascular resistance.
  • Reducing intravascular volume through sodium and water excretion.
  • Changing heart rate or contractility in selected clinical settings.
  • Modulating RAAS activity, which affects both vascular tone and volume.

The medication choice should follow the patient’s physiology and clinical context—not a memorized list of “blood-pressure pills.”

Part 2 — Confirm the Clinical Problem Before Intensifying Therapy

An elevated office reading can reflect inaccurate technique, acute pain, anxiety, stimulant use, white-coat effect, missed doses, volume overload, or an underlying secondary cause. Before escalating a chronic regimen, confirm measurement quality, review home readings when available, assess adherence and access, and look for medications or substances that can raise blood pressure.

Hypertension care is longitudinal. The FNP needs a baseline, a trend, a cardiovascular-risk assessment, a medication reconciliation, and a follow-up plan—not only a single number.

Part 3 — RAAS Review

Reduced effective renal perfusion can activate:

Renin → angiotensin I → ACE → angiotensin II → vasoconstriction + aldosterone release.

Angiotensin II raises systemic vascular resistance. Aldosterone promotes sodium retention and potassium secretion; water follows retained sodium. RAAS-active medications can lower blood pressure by reducing this vascular and volume response.

These same mechanisms explain important monitoring needs: kidney function, potassium, volume status, blood pressure, and symptoms.

Part 4 — ACE Inhibitors

ACE inhibitors reduce formation of angiotensin II. The physiologic result can include less vasoconstriction, less aldosterone signaling, and lower intraglomerular pressure in relevant settings. They are used for hypertension and may have additional roles depending on conditions such as heart failure, diabetes with kidney disease, or cardiovascular disease.

Key safety concepts include hypotension, a rise in potassium, kidney-function changes, cough, and rare but potentially dangerous angioedema. A clinically meaningful change in kidney function must be interpreted with the patient’s volume status, concurrent nephrotoxic exposures, bilateral renal-artery disease risk, and current prescribing guidance—not by a single lab value in isolation.

Part 5 — ARBs

Angiotensin-receptor blockers reduce angiotensin II signaling at its receptor. They share many hemodynamic and monitoring considerations with ACE inhibitors, including potassium and kidney-function assessment. They may be used when an ACE inhibitor is not tolerated for certain reasons, but they are not interchangeable in every individual situation.

A critical safety principle: do not casually combine multiple RAAS blockers. Combining agents that act on the same pathway can increase kidney and potassium-related risk without routinely creating a better primary-care plan.

Part 6 — Pregnancy Potential Is a Medication-Safety Question

RAAS-active drugs have important pregnancy-related safety considerations. Before initiating or continuing a medication in a patient who could become pregnant, use current prescribing information and guideline resources, discuss pregnancy intentions and contraception as clinically appropriate, and select a safer plan when needed.

Do not make this a checkbox. It is shared decision-making, medication safety, and continuity-of-care planning.

Part 7 — Thiazide-Type and Thiazide-Like Diuretics

These agents promote sodium excretion in the distal nephron. Sodium loss decreases extracellular volume and, over time, contributes to lower vascular resistance. They are commonly used in hypertension management, but effectiveness and safety depend on kidney function, volume status, dietary intake, concurrent drugs, and the individual patient.

Monitor for electrolyte disturbances such as low sodium or potassium, volume depletion, dizziness, gout-related risk in susceptible patients, and metabolic effects. A patient who develops weakness, confusion, cramps, orthostasis, or poor intake after a medication change needs a clinical assessment—not automatic refill approval.

Part 8 — Loop Diuretics: Congestion Is Not the Same as Hypertension

Loop diuretics produce more potent natriuresis and are often central to management of clinically significant volume overload, such as congestion in heart failure. They are not simply stronger routine antihypertensives.

Think in hemodynamic terms:

Congestion → increased filling pressures → dyspnea, edema, weight gain, orthopnea.
Diuresis → sodium/water excretion → lower volume and filling pressure → symptom improvement.

Overdiuresis can cause volume depletion, hypotension, AKI, and electrolyte abnormalities. The target is euvolemia and symptom improvement, not indiscriminate fluid removal.

Part 9 — Potassium-Sparing Diuretics and Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonism

Some diuretics reduce potassium loss; mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists oppose aldosterone signaling. These can be useful in specific clinical settings, including some patients with resistant hypertension or heart failure, but they can raise potassium—especially when kidney function is impaired or other potassium-raising drugs are present.

Never think of potassium as an isolated laboratory value. Potassium balance affects cardiac electrophysiology, and severe abnormalities can create urgent arrhythmia risk.

Part 10 — Calcium-Channel Blockers

Calcium-channel blockers are a broad class. Dihydropyridine agents primarily relax arterial smooth muscle and reduce systemic vascular resistance. Non-dihydropyridine agents also have more direct effects on cardiac rate and conduction.

Common clinical reasoning points include peripheral edema, dizziness, headache, constipation with selected agents, bradycardia or conduction concerns with rate-slowing agents, and interactions with other medications. Peripheral edema from arteriolar dilation is not automatically the same as sodium-retention edema; assess the pattern and the whole patient before adding a diuretic reflexively.

Part 11 — Beta Blockers: Indication Matters

Beta blockers reduce sympathetic effects on the heart and can lower heart rate, contractility, and renin release. They are particularly relevant when there is a compelling indication such as selected heart-failure syndromes, prior MI, angina, or certain arrhythmias. They are not a generic substitute for individualized antihypertensive selection.

Monitor heart rate, blood pressure, fatigue, dizziness, bronchospasm risk in susceptible patients, mood or sleep effects, glycemic-awareness concerns, and interactions with other rate-slowing medications. Abrupt discontinuation of some beta blockers can be harmful; medication changes need a supervised plan.

Part 12 — Hypertension Plus CKD, Diabetes, CAD, or Heart Failure

Comorbidities change the treatment question.

  • CKD: assess albuminuria context, kidney function trend, potassium, volume status, and renal-protective indications.
  • Diabetes: consider renal and cardiovascular risk, hypoglycemia awareness, and metabolic effects of the full regimen.
  • CAD/angina or prior MI: heart rate, ischemia, and evidence-based secondary-prevention needs may guide the regimen.
  • Heart failure: distinguish HFrEF from HFpEF, congestion from euvolemia, and disease-modifying therapy from symptom-focused diuresis.

A diagnosis does not automatically determine one medication. It changes the risk-benefit calculation.

Part 13 — Resistant or Apparent Resistant Hypertension

Before labeling a patient “resistant,” reassess technique, adherence, medication access, interacting substances, white-coat effect, volume excess, sleep apnea, kidney disease, endocrine contributors, and regimen adequacy. Apparent treatment resistance can be a measurement, adherence, or secondary-cause problem.

Complex or persistent cases may need team-based care, pharmacy input, specialist consultation, and targeted secondary-hypertension evaluation.

Part 14 — Severe Blood Pressure: Urgency Is About Organ Injury

A markedly elevated reading requires assessment for symptoms and evidence of acute target-organ injury. Concerning findings can include neurologic deficits, encephalopathy, acute chest pain, acute pulmonary edema, aortic-dissection features, severe kidney injury, or pregnancy-related emergency features.

The FNP question is not merely “How high is the pressure?” It is: Is there acute target-organ injury that requires emergency evaluation? A stable patient without acute injury still needs timely, careful outpatient management and close follow-up; do not rapidly lower blood pressure without a clinically appropriate plan.

Part 15 — Monitoring After a Medication Change

Every medication change should specify:

  1. What is the blood-pressure target and how will readings be measured?
  2. What symptoms or home measurements should the patient record?
  3. Which laboratories are needed, and when?
  4. What adverse effects are expected versus urgent?
  5. When will the clinician reassess efficacy, adherence, and safety?

Home blood-pressure monitoring can be highly useful when technique and device selection are appropriate. Ask the patient to bring readings—and sometimes the device—to follow-up rather than relying on memory alone.

Part 16 — Clinical Case: Rising Creatinine and Potassium

A patient with diabetes and CKD begins a RAAS-active medication. On follow-up, blood pressure is improved, but creatinine and potassium have risen.

Do not respond with “the medication is good” or “the medication is bad.” Build the clinical picture:

RAAS effect + baseline kidney reserve + hydration/acute illness + NSAID use + potassium supplements or potassium-sparing medication + trend and symptom assessment.

Review medications, assess volume status and illness, use drug-specific monitoring guidance, and determine whether dose adjustment, temporary hold, urgent evaluation, or coordinated specialty input is needed.

Part 17 — Clinical Case: Edema After a Calcium-Channel Blocker

A patient reports new bilateral ankle swelling after starting a dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker. They have no dyspnea, orthopnea, weight gain, JVD, or pulmonary findings.

Consider medication-related arteriolar vasodilation in the differential. Do not label every edema complaint “heart failure,” and do not reflexively add a diuretic without reassessing the medication, hemodynamics, renal function, and alternative causes.

Part 18 — Clinical Case: Severe Pressure With Neurologic Symptoms

A patient reports a very high home blood-pressure value with new unilateral weakness and difficulty speaking. This is not routine titration.

Possible acute neurologic target-organ injury → emergency evaluation now.

The safest pharmacology decision may be not to prescribe anything in the clinic, but to arrange emergency care and communicate the medication history to the receiving team.

FNP Antihypertensive Framework

  1. Confirm the blood-pressure pattern and measurement quality.
  2. Assess cardiovascular risk, symptoms, organ injury, and secondary contributors.
  3. Choose therapy by mechanism plus compelling indications and patient factors.
  4. Check kidney function, electrolytes, heart rate, volume status, pregnancy potential, and interactions as relevant.
  5. Set a monitoring interval, home plan, laboratory plan, and red flags.
  6. Reassess adherence, adverse effects, cost, and clinical response before escalating.

High-Yield Summary

RAAS-active medications: lower angiotensin-II/aldosterone signaling; monitor kidney function, potassium, blood pressure, and pregnancy-related safety.
Thiazide-type agents: sodium excretion with electrolyte and volume monitoring.
Loop diuretics: primarily manage congestion; avoid overdiuresis.
Calcium-channel blockers: class-specific vascular versus rate/conduction effects; edema has a differential.
Beta blockers: use with indication-driven thinking and rate/conduction monitoring.
Severe pressure: assess for acute target-organ injury and disposition first.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Drug selection, dosing, laboratory monitoring, blood-pressure targets, and pregnancy management must use current guidelines, prescribing information, local scope requirements, and the individual patient’s clinical context.
